newsitem.title: ITALY: FOOD -- UN summit urged to honour hunger vow.
newsitem.headline: FOOD -- UN summit urged to honour hunger vow.

text.p: World nations have ended a summit to tackle hunger, urged on by some to exceed their pledge of halving the number of starving and denounced by others as engaging in a shameful farce that will fail the poor and needy.
Watched by Cuban president Fidel Castro, demonstrators disrupted the start of a final news conference on Sunday to denounce the World Food Summit's stated goals as a sham.
"This is a farce," a woman told the organisers before being dragged from the room in a scuffle between security guards and about half a dozen other demonstrators.
"You are participating in a criminal process," she said, and appeared to stuff part of the summit declaration into her mouth.

The five-day summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation produced a commitment by leaders to try and cut in half the number of hungry people in the world from 840 million now by the year 2015.

Faced with criticism that the summit --like others before it on global crises -- agreed only non-binding commitments and offered no new cash, FAO director general Jacques Diouf urged nations to do more.
He told the news conference that he would have preferred the 186 nations which signed up to the declaration to pledge to eradicate hunger altogether.

"We have made progress but we in the FAO think halving the level of people without access to food to 400 million by 2015 is a minimum objective and we hope that with good will and commitment we should be able to do better and more," he said.
Castro, whose presence upstaged a summit shunned by most rich leaders, defended his decision to call the summit "shameful" because it would still leave millions to die.

"If I had to return to a similar conference I would say the same because the world is full of injustice and the situation is getting worse," he told the 1,000 journalists allowed in to Sunday's news conference.
The veteran communist leader had used his summit speech on Saturday to lash out at capitalism, slamming the agreed goals of the gathering as modest and cosmetic.
The summit at FAO headquarters in Rome, overshadowed by the refugee crisis in Zaire, was the highest level meeting of its kind called to discuss efforts to end starvation.
A World Food Conference in 1974 pledged to wipe out hunger in a decade but the number of people going hungry has barely eased.

The summit had shown that "all together we will work hand in hand to ensure that young children and babies will not cry of hunger and that mothers will not be looking at children who have no hope," Diouf, who is from Senegal, told delegates in Rome.

The summit texts were adopted by acclamation at the start of the gathering after more than two years of negotiation and contain compromise language in contentious areas such as trade, development aid, population, sanctions and women's rights.
The summit was the last in a series of major U.N. conferences over the past four years to map out an agenda for tackling the world's problems on the eve of the 21st century.
